summary: Essex County, NY Adirondack lookout: 1919 steel tower closed after the 1971 season and later removed; cabin gone; public hiking route since a 2012 easement.

facts.design: 47-ft LS40 Aermotor steel fire lookout tower, built 1919 to replace a 1911 wooden tower
facts.status_note: Closed at the end of the 1971 fire lookout season and later removed (date not given); the observer's cabin has also been removed
facts.agency: Conservation Commission (Wikipedia); Forest Lookouts calls it the State Conservation Department

access.note: A 2012 easement from Elk Lake gives the public hiking access along the route (Peakery)

visit.trail_note: Starts at The Branch parking area on Blue Ridge Road; a logging road along the Branch River leads to the former cabin site, then a trail to the summit (Peakery)

events.note: Conservation Commission built a wooden tower on the summit for fire lookout purposes
Conservation Commission replaced the wooden tower with a 47-ft steel LS40 Aermotor tower; a 1943 survey description gives about 60 ft
Joseph Hanmer of Blue Ridge named as the observer stationed on the mountain (September 1919 newspaper)
January 1939 newspaper item names Ernest Hamner as the observer; the start date is not given
Closed at the end of the 1971 fire lookout season because aerial detection had grown; later removed
Elk Lake granted the public an easement for hiking to Boreas Mountain along the existing roads and trail

resolved_conflicts.explanation: Wikipedia says the tower was closed at the end of the 1971 season and was later removed. NCPR, quoting Jeff Mans, says the state removed it in the 1970s. The two fit together, so the record gives 1971 as the closing season and leaves the removal year unstated.

sources.title: Amateur sleuthing led to this weekend's Adirondack Mountain Club hike

notes_for_editor: Height conflict left open: Wikipedia gives 47 ft (14 m) for the 1919 LS40 steel tower, while a 1943 Coast and Geodetic Survey description says about 60 ft with a glass cab. The story reports both and does not choose. The easement and route come from a user-written trail page (Peakery) and were not checked on the ground. The names Hanmer (1919) and Hamner (1939) are spelled differently; the record does not link them. A Facebook post from the NY FFLA chapter, titled 'The site where the observers cabin once stood', appeared in search with a cabin removal year, but it could not be read from cache, so it is not cited and the removal year is not used.
